--- title: "Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering" subtitle: "Learning without labels · K-Means · Choosing k · Hierarchical · DBSCAN · Profiling" --- ::: {.callout-note} **This chapter finds structure in data that has no answer column at all.** **Assumed knowledge:** Session 5 — scaling, and why distance-based methods need it. Session 8 — scatter plots. Session 9 — the `fit` / `predict` shape of a scikit-learn model. **The one idea to take away:** there is **no right answer to check against**. That changes everything: you cannot measure accuracy, so you must justify your result instead. This chapter is mostly about how to justify one. ::: ## 🎯 Learning outcomes {#sec-s10-outcomes} By the end of this chapter you can: 1. Explain how unsupervised learning differs from supervised learning. 2. Describe the K-Means algorithm step by step. 3. Show why clustering must be done on scaled data. 4. Choose *k* using an elbow plot and a silhouette score, and say what to do when they disagree. 5. Use hierarchical clustering and DBSCAN, and say when each beats K-Means. 6. Turn clusters into a description a business can act on. ## How this chapter is organised {#sec-s10-organisation} | Part | Question it answers | |---|---| | [A — Learning without labels](#sec-s10-a) | *What can you learn with no answer key?* | | [B — K-Means](#sec-s10-b) | *How does the standard method actually work?* | | [C — Choosing k](#sec-s10-c) | *How many groups are there?* | | [D — When K-Means fails](#sec-s10-d) | *What do I use instead?* | # Part A — Learning without labels {#sec-s10-a} ## 1. Unsupervised learning {#sec-s10-topic-1} **Unsupervised learning finds structure in data that has no target column.** Nobody has labelled anything; the algorithm has only the features. | | Supervised (Session 9) | Unsupervised (this chapter) | |---|---|---| | Data | `X` **and** `y` | `X` only | | Goal | predict `y` for new rows | find structure in `X` | | Can you measure accuracy? | **yes** — compare to the true `y` | **no** — there is no true answer | | Fails by | predicting badly | producing groups that mean nothing | Three families: | Family | Finds | Covered in | |---|---|---| | **Clustering** | groups of similar rows | this chapter | | **Dimensionality reduction** | a smaller set of columns | Session 6 (PCA) | | **Association rules** | things that occur together | Session 16 | ::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Analogy — sorting the laundry"} Nobody told you the categories. You tip the basket out and start making piles — darks, whites, towels — because things in a pile *resemble* each other. **Somebody else would make different piles.** By fabric, perhaps, or by owner. Neither is wrong. **That is unsupervised learning: several defensible answers, and no marking scheme.** ::: ## 2. What clustering is for {#sec-s10-topic-2} **Clustering puts rows into groups so that rows in a group are more similar to each other than to rows in other groups.** | Use | What the clusters become | |---|---| | Customer segmentation | marketing groups with different offers | | Document grouping | topics | | Image compression | a small palette of representative colours | | Anomaly detection | whatever does not fit any cluster | | Exploration | the first look at data nobody has labelled | **"Similar" means "close together" — so clustering is a distance calculation**, and every warning from Session 5 about scale applies with full force. # Part B — K-Means {#sec-s10-b} ## 3. How K-Means works {#sec-s10-topic-3} **K-Means splits data into *k* groups by repeatedly moving *k* centre points until they settle.** ```{mermaid} flowchart TB S1["1. Pick k. Place k centres at random"] S2["2. Assign every point to its
nearest centre"] S3["3. Move each centre to the average
of the points assigned to it"] S4{"Did anything
move?"} S1 --> S2 --> S3 --> S4 S4 -- yes --> S2 S4 -- no --> S5["Done. The centres have settled"] ``` **You must choose *k* yourself.** The algorithm cannot tell you how many groups exist — that is the whole difficulty, and Part C is about it. ### Demo 1 — watching the centres settle, step by step ::: {#cell-fig-s10-kmeans-steps .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd points = pd.read_csv("datasets/three_blobs.csv")[["x", "y"]].values centres = np.array([[1., 6.], [2., 7.], [3., 6.5]]) # deliberately bad starting positions fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13, 3.1)) for step, ax in enumerate(axes): distances = np.linalg.norm(points[:, None] - centres[None], axis=2) labels = distances.argmin(axis=1) # step 2: assign ax.scatter(points[:, 0], points[:, 1], c=labels, s=12, cmap="viridis") ax.scatter(centres[:, 0], centres[:, 1], c="red", marker="X", s=150, edgecolor="k") ax.set_title(f"iteration {step}", fontsize=10); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]) for j in range(3): # step 3: move if (labels == j).any(): centres[j] = points[labels == j].mean(axis=0) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() print("Started at:", [[1., 6.], [2., 7.], [3., 6.5]], "— all three bunched in one corner") print("Ended at: ", centres.round(1).tolist()) print("The true centres were [2,2], [7,3], [4,7].") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Four iterations of K-Means. The crosses are the centres; watch them walk into place.](session-10-unsupervised-learning-techniques-clustering_files/figure-html/fig-s10-kmeans-steps-output-1.png){#fig-s10-kmeans-steps width=1419 height=330} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Started at: [[1.0, 6.0], [2.0, 7.0], [3.0, 6.5]] — all three bunched in one corner Ended at: [[1.9, 2.0], [4.1, 7.0], [7.0, 3.0]] The true centres were [2,2], [7,3], [4,7]. ``` ::: ::: ### Demo 2 — the same thing with scikit-learn ::: {#cell-fig-s10-kmeans-sklearn .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.cluster import KMeans # A real dataset: 200 mall customers, their annual income and a spending score # the mall assigned them. customers = pd.read_csv("datasets/Mall_Customers.csv").rename(columns={ "Annual Income (k$)": "income", "Spending Score (1-100)": "spending_score"}) print(customers.head(3), f"\n\n{len(customers)} customers on file\n") km = KMeans(n_clusters=5, random_state=0, n_init=10) customers["cluster"] = km.fit_predict(customers[["income", "spending_score"]]) plt.scatter(customers["income"], customers["spending_score"], c=customers["cluster"], cmap="viridis", s=18) plt.scatter(km.cluster_centers_[:, 0], km.cluster_centers_[:, 1], c="red", marker="X", s=220, edgecolor="k", label="centres") plt.xlabel("Annual income (k$)"); plt.ylabel("Spending score"); plt.legend() plt.show() print(customers.groupby("cluster").agg( n=("income", "size"), avg_income=("income", "mean"), avg_spend=("spending_score", "mean") ).round(1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` CustomerID Gender Age income spending_score 0 1 Male 19 15 39 1 2 Male 21 15 81 2 3 Female 20 16 6 200 customers on file ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Customer segments by income and spending score, with the centres marked.](session-10-unsupervised-learning-techniques-clustering_files/figure-html/fig-s10-kmeans-sklearn-output-2.png){#fig-s10-kmeans-sklearn width=682 height=408} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` n avg_income avg_spend cluster 0 81 55.3 49.5 1 39 86.5 82.1 2 35 88.2 17.1 3 23 26.3 20.9 4 22 25.7 79.4 ``` ::: ::: Note `n_init=10`: K-Means starts from random positions and can settle into a poor arrangement, so it runs ten times from different starts and keeps the best. ## 4. Scale first — always {#sec-s10-topic-4} **K-Means measures straight-line distance. An unscaled column with big numbers decides every cluster on its own.** This is Session 5's lesson, and clustering is where it does the most damage — because there is no accuracy score to warn you that the answer is wrong. ### Demo 3 — real data where the scales genuinely differ The mall file happens to be convenient: income in thousands (range 122) and spending score out of 100 (range 98) are already on comparable scales, so scaling would change almost nothing. **Check before you assume you need it.** ::: {#b70caa1c .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd mall = pd.read_csv("datasets/Mall_Customers.csv").rename(columns={ "Annual Income (k$)": "income", "Spending Score (1-100)": "spending_score"}) print("Mall file — the two columns are already comparable:") for c in ["income", "spending_score"]: print(f" {c:<15} range {mall[c].max() - mall[c].min():>10,.0f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Mall file — the two columns are already comparable: income range 122 spending_score range 98 ``` ::: ::: Now a real file where they are not. `loan_data_10k.csv` records **income in rupees** (hundreds of thousands) next to **loan-to-income ratio** (a fraction between 0 and 1). ::: {#cell-fig-s10-scaling .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.cluster import KMeans from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler loan = (pd.read_csv("datasets/loan_data_10k.csv") .dropna(subset=["person_income", "loan_percent_income"]) .sample(2_000, random_state=0)) X = loan[["person_income", "loan_percent_income"]] print("Loan file — the two columns are not remotely comparable:") for c in X.columns: print(f" {c:<22} range {X[c].max() - X[c].min():>13,.2f}") unscaled_labels = KMeans(4, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(X) scaled_labels = KMeans(4, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)) fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6)) ax[0].scatter(X["person_income"], X["loan_percent_income"], c=unscaled_labels, cmap="viridis", s=6, alpha=.6) ax[0].set_title("Unscaled — boundaries are vertical") ax[1].scatter(X["person_income"], X["loan_percent_income"], c=scaled_labels, cmap="viridis", s=6, alpha=.6) ax[1].set_title("Scaled — both columns count") for a in ax: a.set_xlabel("Income (₹)"); a.set_ylabel("Loan as a share of income"); a.set_xscale("log") plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() agree = pd.crosstab(unscaled_labels, scaled_labels).max(axis=1).sum() / len(X) print(f"\nUnscaled, an income gap of ₹1,000 outweighs the entire 0-to-1 ratio scale.") print(f"The two clusterings agree on only {agree:.0%} of applicants —") print(f"{1 - agree:.0%} land in a completely different group depending on whether you scaled.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Loan file — the two columns are not remotely comparable: person_income range 832,912.00 loan_percent_income range 0.53 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Left: unscaled, so income alone decides and the boundaries are vertical. Right: scaled, so both columns count.](session-10-unsupervised-learning-techniques-clustering_files/figure-html/fig-s10-scaling-output-2.png){#fig-s10-scaling width=1198 height=384} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Unscaled, an income gap of ₹1,000 outweighs the entire 0-to-1 ratio scale. The two clusterings agree on only 57% of applicants — 43% land in a completely different group depending on whether you scaled. ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Unscaled clustering produces confident nonsense"} No error is raised. The clusters look tidy, the chart is colourful, and **43% of applicants are in a different group** purely because of a unit choice. **Put `StandardScaler` in front of `KMeans` unless you have checked that the columns are already comparable** — and check by printing the ranges, as the first cell above does. ::: # Part C — Choosing k {#sec-s10-c} ## 5. The elbow method {#sec-s10-topic-5} **Inertia is the total squared distance from every point to its own centre.** More clusters always means lower inertia — with one cluster per point it reaches zero — so you cannot simply minimise it. **The elbow method looks for the point where the improvement stops being worth it.** ### Demo 4 — the elbow ::: {#cell-fig-s10-elbow .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.cluster import KMeans from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(customers[["income", "spending_score"]]) ks = range(1, 9) inertias = [KMeans(k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit(Xs).inertia_ for k in ks] plt.plot(ks, inertias, "o-") plt.axvline(5, color="red", ls="--", alpha=.6) plt.xlabel("k (number of clusters)"); plt.ylabel("inertia") plt.title("Where does the line stop dropping steeply?") plt.show() print(f"{'k':>3} {'inertia':>10} {'improvement':>13}") for i, (k, v) in enumerate(zip(ks, inertias)): imp = "" if i == 0 else f"{(inertias[i-1]-v)/inertias[i-1]:>12.1%}" print(f"{k:>3} {v:>10.1f} {imp:>13}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Inertia falls with every extra cluster. The bend at k=5 is where extra clusters stop paying.](session-10-unsupervised-learning-techniques-clustering_files/figure-html/fig-s10-elbow-output-1.png){#fig-s10-elbow width=681 height=431} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` k inertia improvement 1 400.0 2 269.3 32.7% 3 157.7 41.4% 4 108.9 30.9% 5 65.6 39.8% 6 55.1 15.9% 7 44.9 18.5% 8 37.1 17.3% ``` ::: ::: Read the improvement column: large gains up to k=5, then much smaller ones. **That is the elbow** — and five is the answer this well-known dataset is famous for. ## 6. The silhouette score {#sec-s10-topic-6} **The silhouette score measures, for each point, how much closer it is to its own cluster than to the next nearest one.** It runs from −1 to +1. | Score | Means | |---|---| | **near +1** | comfortably inside its own cluster | | **near 0** | on the boundary — could belong to either | | **negative** | **closer to a different cluster — probably misassigned** | Unlike inertia, it does **not** automatically improve with more clusters, so you can compare values across different *k* directly. ### Demo 5 — silhouette across k ::: {#cell-fig-s10-silhouette .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.cluster import KMeans from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score ks = range(2, 9) scores = [silhouette_score(Xs, KMeans(k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(Xs)) for k in ks] plt.plot(list(ks), scores, "o-", color="darkgreen") best = list(ks)[int(np.argmax(scores))] plt.axvline(best, color="red", ls="--", alpha=.6) plt.xlabel("k"); plt.ylabel("silhouette score"); plt.title("Higher is better") plt.show() for k, s in zip(ks, scores): print(f"k = {k}: silhouette {s:.3f}{' ← best' if k == best else ''}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Silhouette by k. Unlike inertia, higher is genuinely better, so the peak is the answer.](session-10-unsupervised-learning-techniques-clustering_files/figure-html/fig-s10-silhouette-output-1.png){#fig-s10-silhouette width=686 height=431} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` k = 2: silhouette 0.286 k = 3: silhouette 0.467 k = 4: silhouette 0.494 k = 5: silhouette 0.555 ← best k = 6: silhouette 0.538 k = 7: silhouette 0.526 k = 8: silhouette 0.457 ``` ::: ::: Both methods point at the same answer here. **They do not always.** ### Demo 6 — when the silhouette score is wrong ::: {#382036d9 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np from sklearn.cluster import KMeans from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score # Two interleaved crescents. The true structure is obviously 2 groups. mo = pd.read_csv("datasets/moons.csv") moons = mo[["x", "y"]].values true_labels = mo["true_group"].values for k in [2, 3, 4]: labels = KMeans(k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(moons) print(f"k = {k}: silhouette {silhouette_score(moons, labels):.3f}") agree = (KMeans(2, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(moons) == true_labels) print(f"\nAt k=2, K-Means agrees with the true crescents for " f"{max(agree.mean(), 1-agree.mean()):.0%} of points.") print("The score prefers k=2, and yet K-Means still cuts the crescents in the wrong") print("place — because it can only draw straight boundaries. A good score does not") print("mean a good clustering.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` k = 2: silhouette 0.489 k = 3: silhouette 0.428 k = 4: silhouette 0.461 At k=2, K-Means agrees with the true crescents for 76% of points. The score prefers k=2, and yet K-Means still cuts the crescents in the wrong place — because it can only draw straight boundaries. A good score does not mean a good clustering. ``` ::: ::: :::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Clustering always returns clusters"} Ask K-Means for four groups in pure random noise and you will get four groups, each with a centre and a colour, and a chart that looks meaningful. ::: {#2cd3e29e .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np from sklearn.cluster import KMeans from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score noise = pd.read_csv("datasets/random_noise.csv")[["x", "y"]].values # no structure at all for k in [2, 3, 4]: print(f"k = {k} on pure noise: silhouette {silhouette_score(noise, KMeans(k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(noise)):.3f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` k = 2 on pure noise: silhouette 0.314 k = 3 on pure noise: silhouette 0.326 k = 4 on pure noise: silhouette 0.321 ``` ::: ::: Those are not zero. **The elbow and the silhouette are evidence, not proof. The real test is whether the clusters mean something to somebody who knows the business.** :::: ## 7. Profiling: turning clusters into an answer {#sec-s10-topic-7} **A cluster number is not a deliverable.** `cluster = 2` means nothing to a marketing team. The deliverable is a **description**. ### Demo 7 — from cluster numbers to named segments ::: {#5c93d9ee .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from sklearn.cluster import KMeans from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler X = customers[["income", "spending_score"]] customers["segment"] = KMeans(5, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict( StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)) profile = customers.groupby("segment").agg( customers=("income", "size"), median_income=("income", "median"), median_spend=("spending_score", "median"), ).round(0) profile["share"] = (profile["customers"] / len(customers) * 100).round(1).astype(str) + "%" print(profile) print("\nNow name them, and say what to do:") overall_income = customers["income"].median() overall_spend = customers["spending_score"].median() for seg, row in profile.iterrows(): rich = "high" if row["median_income"] > overall_income else "modest" spends = "high" if row["median_spend"] > overall_spend else "low" name = {("high", "high"): "Best customers — reward and retain", ("high", "low"): "Untapped — money, but not spending here", ("modest", "low"): "Budget-conscious — low priority", ("modest", "high"): "Enthusiasts on a budget — grow carefully"}[(rich, spends)] print(f" Segment {seg}: {name:<44} ({row['share']:>5} of customers, " f"${row['median_income']:,.0f}k income)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` customers median_income median_spend share segment 0 81 54.0 50.0 40.5% 1 39 79.0 83.0 19.5% 2 35 85.0 16.0 17.5% 3 23 25.0 17.0 11.5% 4 22 24.0 77.0 11.0% Now name them, and say what to do: Segment 0: Budget-conscious — low priority (40.5% of customers, $54k income) Segment 1: Best customers — reward and retain (19.5% of customers, $79k income) Segment 2: Untapped — money, but not spending here (17.5% of customers, $85k income) Segment 3: Budget-conscious — low priority (11.5% of customers, $25k income) Segment 4: Enthusiasts on a budget — grow carefully (11.0% of customers, $24k income) ``` ::: ::: **That last block is the actual output of a clustering project.** "Segment 1" became "high income, not spending — worth a targeted offer", which somebody can act on tomorrow. # Part D — When K-Means fails {#sec-s10-d} ## 8. Hierarchical clustering {#sec-s10-topic-8} **Hierarchical clustering builds a tree.** It starts with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest, until everything is one cluster. You then cut the tree wherever you like. **Its advantage over K-Means: you do not have to choose *k* in advance.** You build the tree once and read off any number of clusters from it. ### Demo 8 — the dendrogram ::: {#cell-fig-s10-dendro .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import dendrogram, linkage, fcluster from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler sample = customers[["income", "spending_score"]].sample(40, random_state=1) Z = linkage(StandardScaler().fit_transform(sample), method="ward") plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.4)) dendrogram(Z, no_labels=True) plt.axhline(6, color="red", ls="--") plt.ylabel("distance at which clusters merged") plt.title("Cut the tree where the vertical lines are longest") plt.show() for cut in [2, 3, 4]: labels = fcluster(Z, cut, criterion="maxclust") print(f"cutting for {cut} clusters → sizes {np.bincount(labels)[1:].tolist()}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![A dendrogram. Cutting across at a height gives that many clusters — the long vertical gap suggests where.](session-10-unsupervised-learning-techniques-clustering_files/figure-html/fig-s10-dendro-output-1.png){#fig-s10-dendro width=831 height=342} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` cutting for 2 clusters → sizes [9, 31] cutting for 3 clusters → sizes [9, 5, 26] cutting for 4 clusters → sizes [9, 5, 5, 21] ``` ::: ::: ## 9. DBSCAN {#sec-s10-topic-9} **DBSCAN groups points that are packed closely together and labels everything else as noise.** It has two strengths K-Means does not: - clusters can be **any shape**, not just round blobs - points that belong to no cluster are marked as **noise** rather than forced into one You do not give it *k*. You give it `eps` (how close counts as "near") and `min_samples` (how many neighbours make a dense region). ### Demo 9 — the crescents, where K-Means could not win ::: {#cell-fig-s10-dbscan .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, DBSCAN mo = pd.read_csv("datasets/moons.csv") moons, truth = mo[["x", "y"]].values, mo["true_group"].values km_labels = KMeans(2, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(moons) db_labels = DBSCAN(eps=0.2, min_samples=5).fit_predict(moons) fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.2)) ax[0].scatter(*moons.T, c=truth, cmap="viridis", s=10); ax[0].set_title("The truth") ax[1].scatter(*moons.T, c=km_labels, cmap="viridis", s=10); ax[1].set_title("K-Means") ax[2].scatter(*moons.T, c=db_labels, cmap="viridis", s=10); ax[2].set_title("DBSCAN") for a in ax: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([]) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() km_acc = max((km_labels == truth).mean(), 1 - (km_labels == truth).mean()) db_acc = max((db_labels == truth).mean(), 1 - (db_labels == truth).mean()) print(f"K-Means matches the true crescents: {km_acc:.0%}") print(f"DBSCAN matches the true crescents: {db_acc:.0%}") print(f"DBSCAN labelled {(db_labels == -1).sum()} points as noise (label -1)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![K-Means cuts the crescents with a straight line. DBSCAN follows their shape.](session-10-unsupervised-learning-techniques-clustering_files/figure-html/fig-s10-dbscan-output-1.png){#fig-s10-dbscan width=1309 height=341} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` K-Means matches the true crescents: 76% DBSCAN matches the true crescents: 100% DBSCAN labelled 0 points as noise (label -1) ``` ::: ::: ### Demo 10 — choosing between the three ::: {#4f6345ff .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(f"{'':<22} {'K-Means':<22} {'Hierarchical':<22} {'DBSCAN'}") rows = [ ("must choose k?", "yes", "no — cut the tree", "no"), ("cluster shapes", "round blobs only", "flexible", "any shape"), ("handles noise", "no — forces a group", "no", "yes, explicitly"), ("speed on big data", "fast", "slow (n² memory)", "medium"), ("clusters of very different density", "poor", "fair", "poor"), ("main use", "the default first try","exploring structure","odd shapes, outliers"), ] for label, a, b, c in rows: print(f"{label:<22} {a:<22} {b:<22} {c}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` K-Means Hierarchical DBSCAN must choose k? yes no — cut the tree no cluster shapes round blobs only flexible any shape handles noise no — forces a group no yes, explicitly speed on big data fast slow (n² memory) medium clusters of very different density poor fair poor main use the default first try exploring structure odd shapes, outliers ``` ::: ::: ### ❓ Check yourself **Q1.** What makes clustering unsupervised? - (a) It is less accurate. - (b) **There is no target column, so there is no correct answer to compare against.** - (c) It runs without training. **Q2.** Why does inertia always fall as *k* rises? - (a) A bug in scikit-learn. - (b) **More centres means every point is nearer to one, until with one centre per point inertia is zero.** - (c) It does not. **Q3.** You cluster income (in rupees) and age (in years) without scaling. What happens? - (a) Nothing important. - (b) **Income decides every cluster, because its numbers are thousands of times larger.** - (c) The code raises an error. **Q4.** Your data forms two interlocking crescents. Which method? - (a) K-Means with k=2. - (b) **DBSCAN.** - (c) K-Means with k=4. **Q5.** The silhouette score for your clustering is 0.61, and the business says the segments make no sense.
